synopsis: Ray tracing follows light, radio or sound rays through a scene; radar shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) sums multiple reflections, enabling multipath ghosts and Doppler effects rather than treating every surface hit as a detection [f12952, f12953, f12956]. The corpus identifies ray-traced lidar using the actual scan pattern and full signal chain as the best-validated sensor-model type, reporting errors of 1.7% for amplitude, 8.5% for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity only when processing and sensor imperfections were included [f12955, f4417]. Radar material models improve agreement with real images, but Sim2Radar (February 2026), using standard 77 GHz material values in five indoor scenes, produced only about 12% of real point density—251 versus 2,057 points per frame—so ray tracing alone does not guarantee fidelity [f4531, f3931, f4305, f13191]. Transfer to untested machines or mounting positions depends on known materials and sensor internals; reliable 77 GHz material values were lacking in one on-road study, heavy precipitation increases errors, and the booklet's most directly relevant heavy-machine result was RadaRays tested on a wheel loader in a hall [f12964, f12958, f4530, f12959, f15952]. Whole-quarry full-wave simulation is considered impractical, motivating combinations of ray tracing, approximations and statistical electronics models, but no published scene-scale benchmark comparing full-wave simulation with modern real-time radar ray tracers was found [f4536, f4537]. Available tools include dSPACE AURELION and Chrono::Sensor; runtime examples range from 14 hours for a 12-second CPU scenario to about 12 ms per GPU frame and 7.8–18.8 ms per independent ray-traced image, and the corpus explicitly warns against using these as planning constants [f8446, f8495, f12960, f12961, f12962, f12963].
